theme: Deborah and Barak; the song of Deborah
readingInstruction: Read Judges 4:1-5:31. The reading includes the story of Deborah and Barak in prose (chapter 4) and a poem of victory (chapter 5). Notice the two women, Deborah and Jael, who play central roles in a book that is otherwise dominated by men. Read the Song of Deborah aloud, if you can.
settingTheScene: The cycle of Judges continues. After Ehud’s rest, Israel again does evil, and God sells them into the hand of Jabin, a king of Canaan who reigns in Hazor, with a commander named Sisera and nine hundred iron chariots. For twenty years he oppresses Israel. Then comes a remarkable judge, Deborah, a prophetess who sits under a palm tree and settles disputes. She summons Barak, and the story that follows is about courage, hesitation, and the surprising ways God works. The poem in chapter 5 is one of the oldest in the Bible. It celebrates the victory and also names who joined the battle and who stayed home.
observation: Deborah is a prophetess and judge who holds court “under the palm of Deborah” in the hill country of Ephraim (4:4-5).
She tells Barak that the LORD commands him to gather ten thousand men to Mount Tabor, and promises to give Sisera into his hand (4:6-7).
Barak says, “If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go” (4:8).
Deborah replies that the honor will go to a woman, and the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman (4:9).
“The LORD routed Sisera and all his chariots and all his army” (4:15).
Sisera flees on foot to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, who gives him milk, covers him, and drives a tent peg through his temple (4:17-21).
The Song of Deborah praises the LORD who “marched from Seir,” and notes that the stars fought from heaven and the river Kishon swept the enemy away (5:4-5, 20-21).
The song blesses Jael above women and curses Meroz for not coming to the help of the LORD (5:23-24).
interpretation:
Deborah is one of the most striking figures in the book. In a world dominated by male warriors, God raises up a woman as a prophet and judge. She does not lead the army herself, but she delivers the word of the LORD, and her authority is recognized by Barak and the tribes. Her role should remind us that God is not bound by cultural expectations about whom he will use, and that the gifts of prophecy and wisdom come from him.

Barak’s hesitation is also instructive. God has already spoken, and the promise is clear. Yet Barak says he will not go without Deborah. His reluctance is not necessarily cowardice. It may show how much he depends on God’s presence through the prophet. But it costs him. The honor of the final blow will go to a woman. The story then contains a reversal: the conquering general of the iron chariots is brought down by a Kenite woman in a tent.

The battle itself is told briefly. God routs Sisera and his army, and the poem fills in the detail: the stars fought, and the river Kishon swept them away. The text gives the glory to God. The mighty chariots, the Canaanites’ most powerful weapon, are neutralized by a flood. Yet again, God shows that victory does not depend on military strength.

Jael’s act is both shocking and ambiguous. She welcomes a fleeing enemy with hospitality and then kills him in his sleep. The narrator does not condemn or praise her explicitly in chapter 4, but the song in chapter 5 blesses her. She has chosen sides, as an outsider who aligned herself with the people of God. Like Rahab, she is a non-Israelite who joins God’s side. We need not imitate her method. The point is that God uses unexpected people.

The Song of Deborah is a masterwork of praise. It begins with the LORD marching from Seir, a reminder of Sinai, and credits God with the whole victory. It lists the tribes who volunteered and those who stayed behind. Reuben “had great searchings of heart” but remained among the sheepfolds. Meroz is cursed for not coming “to the help of the LORD.” The song shows that the people of God are summoned to take part in his work, and neutrality is not an option.

The final line of the song is a prayer: “So may all your enemies perish, O LORD! But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might.” The victory of God’s people is a picture of the final victory of Christ, the true seed of the woman who crushes the head of the serpent (Genesis 3:15). Sisera’s death by a woman’s hand is a small echo of that promise.
connection: The defeat of Jabin and Hazor recalls Joshua 11. The Song of Deborah parallels the Song of Moses (Exodus 15) and Hannah’s song (1 Samuel 2). The imagery of the LORD marching from Seir is also in Deuteronomy 33:2 and Habakkuk 3:3-6. The crushing of the head echoes Genesis 3:15, and Mary’s Magnificat in Luke 1:46-55 follows the same pattern of reversal. Jael is mentioned in Judges 5 as “most blessed of women,” a phrase later applied to Mary in Luke 1:42.
application:
First, think about the ways you hesitate to obey. Like Barak, we may say yes to God, but only if some condition is met. Ask yourself whether you are waiting for something God has not promised before you obey.

Second, be willing to take part. The song blesses those who came and warns those who stayed behind. Is there a need in your church that you have been standing back from? Offer your time or talent in one specific way.

Third, learn from Deborah. She exercised her gift without apology and gave God the glory. Whatever your gifting, use it in service.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he uses unexpected people.
Confess where you have hesitated to obey him.
Ask him to help you join his work today.
